app.js vs. server.js: One Job Each

Why building the app and running it are split into two files, instead of one.

There's no Laravel equivalent to point at here — artisan serve and the framework bootstrapping are both hidden from you. This project makes that bootstrapping an explicit, deliberate two-file split:

  • app.js — builds the Express app: creates it, registers every app.use(...) (Figure 1.3, previous slide), and exports the finished app. It never starts listening for real requests.
  • server.js — imports that app and is the only place that calls app.listen(...), actually opening a port and starting the live process.

Why bother separating "define what the app does" from "run it"? Because app.js's export is then just a plain, fully-configured Express app object — something else can use it without ever binding a real network port. Right now nothing else does. But this project introduces automated tests starting Week 3, and by Week 6 those tests call routes directly against the exported app (via a library called supertest) rather than starting a real server and making real HTTP requests over the network — faster, and with no risk of port conflicts between test runs. None of that needs to make sense yet; the point for now is just that the split exists because app.js on its own is a reusable, listen-free thing.

server.js's own job — reading which port to listen on — is covered properly in this lesson's Configuration topic, once process.env has been introduced.
